scenario: What if everyone in the UK received £1 million tomorrow?

simulation.scenario_title: Everyone in the UK Gets £1 Million
simulation.summary: Every UK resident receives £1 million overnight. Money supply jumps enormously while goods, housing and labour stay the same, so what money can buy becomes the central question.
assumptions: The payment is real, one-off and universally known.
Production capacity does not change overnight.
Banks and markets keep operating, at least initially.
No coordinated international response at first.

timeline.headline: Shock and scramble
timeline.summary: Banking systems strain and shops, estate agents and markets react within hours.
consequences: Payment systems and banking apps struggle under demand.
Sellers raise prices or pull stock.
Many people stop turning up to work.
Sterling falls sharply as markets react.

timeline.headline: Inflation and labour shortages
timeline.summary: Demand far outstrips supply, so prices surge, especially for housing and scarce services.
consequences: Severe inflation as spending chases limited goods.
Shortages of care, trades, hospitality and transport workers.
Imports surge, putting pressure on the currency.
Government faces pressure for price controls and rationing.

timeline.headline: A reshaped economy
timeline.summary: The one-off gain is largely absorbed, but the economy and social structure may look very different.
consequences: Real value of £1m is much lower than at first.
Wage structures and automation investment shift.
Wealth gaps may re-emerge in new forms.
Migration and trade patterns change.

key_effects: Prices rise rapidly as demand outstrips supply.
Pressure on sterling and trade balances.
second_order_effects: Sudden demand for care and trades at very high pay.
Rapid investment in automation to replace scarce workers.
benefits: Large short-term freedom to retrain or start businesses.
Debt and housing stress relieved for many.

decisions.title: Spend it immediately
decisions.description: Most people spend the bulk of the money within weeks.

decisions.title: Invest it
decisions.description: Most people put the money into property, shares and businesses.

decisions.title: Release it gradually
decisions.description: Government restricts access and distributes the money over years.

branch.decision_explanation: The government locks the funds and pays them out in small monthly instalments over a decade.
branch.how_it_differs: Demand rises steadily instead of exploding, so inflation is far milder and supply can adjust, though public trust and enforcement become the main strain.

timeline.headline: Relief and frustration
timeline.summary: People are told the money exists but cannot spend it all at once.
consequences: Large queues and political protests demanding access.
Black markets for early access appear.
Markets calm compared with the unrestricted case.

timeline.headline: Managed boom
timeline.summary: Steady extra spending lifts the economy with moderate inflation.
consequences: Prices rise but far more slowly.
Fewer workers quit, easing shortages.
Housing demand grows but lending is controlled.

timeline.headline: Gradual transformation
timeline.summary: The economy adjusts to higher incomes, with productivity and investment gradually growing.
consequences: Higher living standards, spread over time.
Trust in government is tested by enforcement.
Inequality persists but is narrower.
losers: Anyone excluded by rules or loopholes

benefits: Time for markets and supply to adapt.
